claim: The comment asserts that on 3.11 `asyncio.wait_for` returns a slot granted in the same tick as a cancellation (so a cancelled call would run), and implies `asyncio.timeout` plus `Semaphore.acquire` does not.

# Not asyncio.wait_for: on 3.11 it returns a slot granted in the same
        # tick as a cancellation, so a cancelled call would run anyway.

claim: The module docstring asserts the slot limit, wait limit and saturation warning assume one event loop at a time, that a second concurrent loop's calls get their own slots and can together exceed the executor's threads, and that the extra calls wait in the shared executor queue where neither the wait limit nor the warning applies.
source_excerpt:
- The slot limit, the wait limit and the saturation warning assume every SQL
  call runs on one event loop at a time, as the server does. Calls from a
  second loop running at the same time get their own slots, so together the
  loops can admit more calls than the executor has threads; the extra calls
  wait in the shared executor's queue, where neither the wait limit nor the
  warning applies.
verify_against: `_slots` (WeakKeyDictionary keyed by loop), `_get_executor` and `run_blocking_sql` in sql_threads.py; the server's event-loop setup in src/sqllens/server.py and src/sqllens/transport/http.py
verify_hint: Trace the input: two loops each with 8 calls in flight; confirm `_slots` gives each loop its own Semaphore, the single `_executor` has 8 workers, and nothing times out a submitted future. Also check whether the server ever runs SQL from another loop (e.g. `asyncio.run` in CLI verify-memory or a worker thread).
